summary:
**ECHOES OF THE UNKNOWN** is an interactive educational game that turns NASA mission history into a story-driven exploration experience. Players investigate three real robotic missions—Surveyor 3, Sojourner, and Opportunity—by exploring mission archives, viewing NASA photographs, reading scientific records, and answering evidence-based questions to recover each archive.

After collecting all three, they can take a final knowledge challenge, review explanations, track their scores, and earn achievements.

The project addresses the challenge by connecting each piece of equipment to its original purpose, scientific contribution, mission lifetime, and lasting legacy. It shows that even when a spacecraft stops operating, its images, measurements, and scientific data can remain valuable for future research.

The fictional archive storyline is clearly distinguished from real mission facts, which are linked to NASA references. Available in English, Bahasa Melayu, and Simplified Chinese, the game makes space history more accessible and engaging.
details:
ECHOES OF THE UNKNOWN (Mission File // EA-03) is an interactive, story-driven space-history web application and educational game exploring NASA robotic missions on the Moon and Mars. Built as an independent student learning prototype aligned with the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge (NASA's Discarded Equipment Storytelling), the project transforms historical NASA mission records and photographs into a playable expedition.

What It Does and How It Works

The application places the player in the role of a Mission Control investigator responding to a fictional incoming archive signal from deep space. Players progress through a structured, multi-stage learning loop:

  • Mission Briefing: Introduces the central question—"What remains after a mission ends?"—and establishes the distinction between the fictional framing signal and verified NASA historical records.
  • Interactive Mission Map: Allows players to explore three historic robotic explorers in any order: Surveyor 3 (Moon, 1967), Sojourner / Mars Pathfinder (Mars, 1997), and Opportunity (Mars, 2004–2019).
  • Archive Investigation & Evidence Scanner: At each destination, players inspect NASA mission photography, key metrics, timelines, and scientific findings. Before unlocking each archive and earning its corresponding badge (Lunar Pioneer, First Rover Step, or Endurance Explorer), players must pass a short knowledge check via an interactive Evidence Scanner modal.
  • Archive Board: Presents a side-by-side comparison table contrasting each spacecraft's destination, mission role, scientific contribution, and end-of-mission status.
  • Flight Simulator (Final Challenge): Recovering all three archives unlocks a customizable timed quiz drawn at random from a 49-question bank built around 14 official NASA Space Apps resources. Players configure difficulty (Cadet, Pilot, or Commander), topic (All, Moon, Mars, or Beyond), and run length (10, 15, or 20 questions). The simulator includes a 50:50 lifeline, speed and streak point multipliers, XP rank progression, unlockable achievements, a local leaderboard, and a personalized mistake log for targeted review.
  • Sources & Transparency Hub: Provides direct links to original NASA/JPL mission pages, image records, technical reports, and audio credits so players can verify every claim.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Active Visual Learning: Rather than functioning as a static text archive or simple trivia quiz, the project pairs real NASA photography (such as Apollo 12 visiting Surveyor 3 and Opportunity's 354-image final panorama) with structured scientific context.
  • Reframing "Discarded" Hardware: It demonstrates that while robotic landers and rovers eventually cease operations on distant worlds, their engineering tests, returned components, and scientific datasets remain active, valuable resources for decades.
  • Scientific Literacy and Critical Thinking: Built-in callouts teach players to evaluate evidence carefully—such as distinguishing geological evidence of ancient liquid water from proof of microbial life, and comparing planned mission lifespans (e.g., 7 sols for Sojourner; 90 sols for Opportunity) against actual operational endurance.
  • Broad Accessibility: Because it runs offline in a single file and supports three languages, it can be used reliably in classrooms, workshops, or areas with limited internet connectivity.

Tools, Languages, and Software Used

The project is engineered as a self-contained, single-file web application requiring no external servers or frameworks:

  • HTML5: Semantic structure (<main>, <section>, <figure>, <nav>), ARIA live regions, progress bars, and modal dialogs for screen-reader accessibility.
  • CSS3: Custom properties, CSS Grid, Flexbox, responsive media queries (supporting screens from 320px mobile viewports up to wide desktops), keyframe animations, and backdrop-filter glassmorphism for a NASA Mission Control aesthetic.
  • JavaScript & HTML5 Canvas: Client-side state management, dynamic quiz randomization, scoring/XP logic, browser-based progress saving, and <canvas> layers (#stars and #fx) for animated deep-space starfields and visual effects.
  • Embedded Audio: Offline background music ("Exploration Theme" by Cleyton Kauffman via OpenGameArt) encoded directly as a Base64 MP3 data URI inside an HTML5 <audio> player with custom volume and hide/reopen controls.

Creativity and Design Approach

  • Narrative Framing ("Signal Recovery"): Using a fictional deep-space transmission as a storytelling hook turns archival reading into an investigative mission while keeping the underlying science strictly factual.
  • Mission Control Interface: Visual elements like an animated boot-up sequence, orbital radar illustrations, HUD signal readouts, and telemetry-style status tags create an authentic aerospace atmosphere.
  • Balanced Gamification: Features like the Evidence Scanner gate, XP ranks, streak bonuses, and the mistake-review mode reward comprehension and reflection rather than blind guessing.

Key Factors Considered

  • Historical Rigor & Source Verification: All dates, measurements, and discoveries were cross-checked against NASA Science and JPL records—even noting minor discrepancies between sources (such as NASA Science listing 6,326 Surveyor 3 TV images versus the 1967 JPL report listing 6,315, resulting in the project's accurate use of "more than 6,300").
  • Multilingual Inclusivity: Full offline localization was built in for English, Bahasa Melayu, and Simplified Chinese via an integrated language selector.
  • Accessibility & Ergonomics: The interface enforces 44px minimum touch targets for mobile usability, high-contrast focus outlines for keyboard navigation, and @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) rules to disable animations for motion-sensitive users.
  • Offline Resilience & Graceful Fallbacks: Embedding the audio directly into the HTML and adding onerror fallbacks with direct NASA source links on every photograph ensures the application remains functional even if external image hosts are unreachable.
  • Ethical Attribution: Clear disclaimers identify the project as an independent student prototype with no implied NASA endorsement, alongside explicit credits for every NASA/JPL team and asset creator.
